prompt: Why is a client secret pasted into a repository's settings a problem even when the logs mask it?
hint: What does whoever holds the string become?

choices.text: Masking slows every workflow run down
choices.why: Masking costs nothing noticeable; the problem is what the string is.

choices.text: Any copy of it is the identity, from anywhere, for months
choices.why: Right. It is long-lived and not bound to the workflow it was meant for.

choices.text: GitHub can read secrets and use them for its own deployments
choices.why: That is not the risk this lesson describes; the risk is every copy, wherever it went.

choices.text: Secrets stored in GitHub expire after one day
choices.why: They do not; a client secret lives until its own expiry, often a year or two.

prompt: The team wants to revoke the client secret used by the shop's deployments. What makes that risky?
hint: What records where the secret is used?

choices.text: Revoking a secret also deletes the app registration
choices.why: The registration stays; only that credential goes.

choices.text: Azure takes a week to honour a revocation
choices.why: Revocation takes effect for new sign-ins quickly; the question is who signs in with it.

choices.text: Nothing records which workflows or machines hold a copy
choices.why: Right. Revoking is a guess about what breaks.

choices.text: A revoked secret is still accepted by the command line
choices.why: Entra ID refuses it; the command line has no say.

prompt: Put the steps of a federated sign-in from a GitHub workflow in order.
hint: GitHub signs first; Azure answers last.
items: The run asks GitHub's token service for an OIDC token
GitHub returns a token naming the repository and environment
The run presents the token to Microsoft Entra ID
Entra ID matches issuer, subject and audience to a federated credential
Entra ID returns an Azure token for the service principal
trap: Putting the match before the token exists is the slip: there is nothing to compare until GitHub has signed one.

prompt: What does Entra ID need stored in advance to accept GitHub's token?
hint: Three facts on the app registration.

choices.text: A copy of GitHub's private signing key
choices.why: It needs GitHub's public keys, which it fetches from the issuer; nobody shares a private key.

choices.text: A federated credential: issuer, subject, audience
choices.why: Right. That is the whole of the trust, and it holds no secret.

choices.text: A client secret with a short expiry
choices.why: Federation stores no secret at all; that is its point.

choices.text: The runner's IP range, so that just GitHub's machines get in
choices.why: Nothing in the exchange checks an address; the signature and the subject do the work.

prompt: For GitHub's token, the federated credential's audience is api://AzureADToken___.
hint: The last word of the audience Azure's documentation fixes.

prompt: A credential trusts `repo:example-shop/shop-api:ref:refs/heads/main`. Next week someone adds a linting workflow on main. What can it do?
hint: Who does a branch subject trust?

choices.text: Sign in as the deploying identity
choices.why: Right. Every job on main produces that subject, so the linter is trusted too.

choices.text: Nothing, because the credential names the deploy workflow's file
choices.why: The default subject names the repository and the ref, not the workflow file.

choices.text: Read the subscription, since linting needs no write role
choices.why: Roles belong to the identity, not to what a job intends to do.

choices.text: Deploy once a reviewer approves the lint job
choices.why: Reviewers belong to environments, and this job names none.

prompt: The deploy job used to name `environment: production`. Someone removes that line, and the login step now fails with AADSTS700213. Why?

choices.text: Removing the environment also removes `id-token: write`
choices.why: Permissions are declared separately; without them the token request would fail earlier, on GitHub's side.

choices.text: The subject changed to the branch form, which no credential trusts
choices.why: Right. Without an environment GitHub uses `ref:refs/heads/main`, and the match is exact.

choices.text: Entra ID refuses tokens from jobs with no environment
choices.why: It accepts any subject that has a credential; this one has none.

choices.text: The client id must be stored as a secret when there is no environment
choices.why: The ids are never secrets and their storage does not change the subject.

prompt: A public repository's maintainers want pull requests to run integration tests against Azure. Which design is safe?
hint: Whose code does a pull request's workflow run?

choices.text: Trust `pull_request` on the production identity, read-only
choices.why: Read-only is not harmless on production, and it is one role change from writable.

choices.text: Store a client secret for pull requests only
choices.why: A long-lived secret reachable by code from forks is the worst of both.

choices.text: A separate identity with a reader role on a separate resource group
choices.why: Right. Pull requests run anybody's code, so they get nothing that reaches production.

choices.text: Trust `ref:refs/heads/*` so every branch is covered
choices.why: Subjects have no wildcards; the comparison is exact.

prompt: Match each job to the subject GitHub puts in its token.
hint: The environment, when there is one, wins.

pairs.left: A push to main, no environment

prompt: Which line lets the job ask GitHub for an OIDC token at all?

choices.text: `environment: production`
choices.why: That changes the subject and adds protections; it does not grant the token.

choices.text: `id-token: write`
choices.why: Right. Without it the login action fails before Azure is involved.

choices.text: `contents: read`
choices.why: That lets checkout read the code.

choices.text: `client-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}`
choices.why: That names the identity to exchange the token for; it does not obtain a token.

prompt: Someone posts the shop's client id, tenant id and subscription id in a public issue. What can a stranger do with them?
hint: Do they name an identity or prove one?

choices.text: Sign in as the identity from any machine
choices.why: Signing in needs a token whose subject matches; ids prove nothing.

choices.text: Deploy to the staging slot, but not production
choices.why: Neither: the ids grant no access anywhere.

choices.text: Read the resource group's resources
choices.why: Reading also needs a token for an identity with a role.

choices.text: Nothing that signs in
choices.why: Right. They name the identity; only a matching signed token proves it, which is why they sit in `vars`.

prompt: The shop's staging deploys and production deploys run in the same workflow, as two jobs. How many federated credentials and identities does the lesson's design use?
hint: A compromised staging run should have nothing to sign in as in production.

choices.text: One identity with one credential for the workflow's file
choices.why: The default subject does not name a file, and one identity would reach both resource groups.

choices.text: Two identities, each with one credential for its environment
choices.why: Right. Each trusts one environment and holds a role on one resource group.

choices.text: One identity with two credentials, one per environment
choices.why: Both environments would then sign in as the same principal, with the same roles.

choices.text: None: the jobs share the login of the first one
choices.why: Each job runs on its own runner and signs in on its own.

prompt: Which changes make the shop's deploy workflow safer? Choose all that apply.
hint: Smaller roles, exact subjects, pinned code.

choices.text: Pinning azure/login to a commit instead of a tag
choices.why: Yes. A tag can be moved by its owner; a commit cannot.

choices.text: Requiring reviewers on the production environment
choices.why: Yes. Then only reviewed runs produce the subject the credential trusts.

choices.text: Moving the client id into `secrets`
choices.why: It changes nothing: the id was never a credential.

choices.text: Giving the identity Contributor on rg-shop instead of Owner on the subscription
choices.why: Yes. Federation removes the secret, not the permissions.

choices.text: Trusting `pull_request` as well, so deploys are tested earlier
choices.why: That opens production to code from any pull request.
